segments.speaker: Sofia Marchetti
segments.text: Design question. Multi-tenant ingest, tenants vary by a factor of about two hundred in volume, and one tenant's burst must not degrade another's. Where do you start?

segments.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
segments.text: I would start with the noisy-neighbour problem rather than the ingest problem, because ingest is mostly solved. Two approaches - per-tenant queues with weighted fair scheduling, or admission control at the edge with per-tenant token buckets. I would do both, but the token bucket first because it is cheap and it fails safe.

segments.speaker: Sofia Marchetti
segments.text: What does fail safe mean there?

segments.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
segments.text: It means when the system is confused, it sheds the largest tenant first rather than the smallest. Most implementations get that backwards and end up protecting whoever is shouting loudest.

segments.speaker: Dan Okafor
segments.text: That is a good answer. What breaks first at ten times the load?

segments.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
segments.text: Metadata, not data. Everyone plans for the bytes and nobody plans for the key space. Tenant count times partition count times retention is usually what falls over, and it falls over as a slow death rather than an outage, which makes it harder to catch.

segments.speaker: Sofia Marchetti
segments.text: How would you catch it?

segments.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
segments.text: A synthetic load test that grows tenant count rather than throughput. Almost nobody runs that because it is boring and it does not look impressive on a slide.

segments.speaker: Dan Okafor
segments.text: Incident question, and I want a real one. Tell me about a time you were the incident commander and it went badly.

segments.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
segments.text: Last March. We lost a region for about two hours. The technical fix took twenty minutes. The other hundred minutes were us arguing about whether to fail over, because nobody had authority to make the call and the person who did was unreachable.

segments.speaker: Dan Okafor
segments.text: What did you change afterwards?

segments.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
segments.text: Two things. We wrote down explicitly who can declare a failover, and it is the on-call engineer, not a VP. And we made the failover a rehearsed monthly event so that declaring it is boring. The second one mattered more. People do not take an action in a crisis that they have never taken before.

segments.speaker: Sofia Marchetti
segments.text: Did anyone push back on giving that authority to on-call?

segments.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
segments.text: Enormously. Two directors were genuinely uncomfortable. What settled it was that on-call made a bad call in a rehearsal in month two and it cost us nothing, which proved the blast radius was survivable.
